title: Birds of Prey
objective: After this level you can describe eagles, hawks and falcons.
summary: Birds of prey share hooked beaks and talons. Eagles and hawks kill with their feet; falcons bite, using a notch on the beak. A trained peregrine was clocked at 242 mph in a 1999 dive.

cards.headline: In 1999, a falcon was clocked at 242 mph.
cards.body: Her name was Frightful, a trained peregrine, diving from nearly three miles up. She belongs to a group of birds built for one job: catching other animals. What turns a bird into a hunter?

cards.headline: Hooks and talons
cards.body: All birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and sharp, curved claws called talons. The daytime hunters (hawks, eagles, vultures and falcons) are also called raptors. The night shift belongs to the owls, and they get the next level. Spot the hooked beak and the talons, and you've found a bird of prey.

cards.headline: Two ways to finish the job

items.label: Eagles and hawks
points: Squeeze prey, like a python's coils

items.label: Falcons
points: Often kill with a bite to the neck
Use a notch on the beak: the 'tomial tooth'

cards.fact: Frightful's speed was measured by a chip on her tail.
cards.context: Falconer Ken Franklin skydived alongside her, and a small chip on her tail feathers recorded the dives. Some falcon experts called the setup artificial, since wild peregrines don't usually start that high. Audubon's field guide is more careful: in a power dive, a peregrine may possibly reach 200 mph. Even the cautious number is astonishing for a bird.

cards.headline: Birds of prey: explained
learned: All share hook-tipped beaks and talons
Eagles and hawks kill by squeezing with their feet
Falcons bite, using the notched 'tomial tooth'

questions.prompt: How fast was the trained peregrine Frightful clocked in her 1999 dives?

options.label: 62 mph
options.rationale: Far too slow; she was clocked at 242 mph.

options.label: 124 mph
options.rationale: About half of her measured speed.

options.label: 424 mph
options.rationale: Faster than any bird has been measured.

questions.explanation: Frightful was clocked at 242 mph (about 389 km/h) diving from nearly three miles up.

questions.prompt: How does a falcon usually kill differently from an eagle or a hawk?

options.label: It bites the neck with a notched beak
It squeezes prey hard with its feet
options.rationale: That's how eagles and hawks do it.

options.label: It drops prey from a great height

questions.explanation: Eagles and hawks constrict prey with their feet; falcons often finish with a bite, using the tomial tooth.

questions.prompt: Level 21 said no bird has teeth. So what is a falcon's 'tomial tooth'?

options.label: A real tooth that only falcons keep
A hatching tooth it never loses
options.rationale: That's a different structure, and chicks lose it.

options.label: An extra-large talon on each foot
options.rationale: Talons are claws on the feet.

options.label: A notched ridge on the upper beak

questions.explanation: The tomial tooth is a sharp notched ridge on the beak, not a tooth; birds have none.
